entities.name: Joannes Maxentius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Joannes Maxentius, a pivotal, albeit often misunderstood, figure in early 6th-century Byzantine theological disputes, emerged as the leading spokesman for the so-called Scythian monks. Active primarily between 519 and 520 CE, Maxentius championed a specific Christological formula, 'one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh' (unus de Trinitate passus est in carne), aiming to reconcile the divisive aftermath of the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE). His efforts, while initially met with suspicion and papal rejection, ultimately laid groundwork for later imperial and ecclesiastical attempts to unify the Eastern Christian world around a refined Chalcedonian orthodoxy.

Maxentius and his fellow Scythian monks, likely from Scythia Minor, arrived in Constantinople in 519 CE, advocating their 'Theopaschite' formula as a bulwark against Nestorianism and a bridge to Monophysite factions. They argued that by asserting the divine person of Christ (one of the Trinity) truly suffered, the formula affirmed the unity of Christ's person while acknowledging his dual nature. This stance brought them into direct conflict with influential theologians and Emperor Justin I, leading to an appeal to Pope Hormisdas in Rome in 520 CE. Despite Maxentius's eloquent defense, Hormisdas, cautious of novel theological language and wary of its potential Monophysite interpretations, condemned the formula, sending the monks back to the East.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Joannes Maxentius, through his fervent advocacy for the Theopaschite formula, played a crucial, though initially unacknowledged, role in the evolution of Chalcedonian Christology. His work contributed to the eventual acceptance of the formula 'one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh' at the Second Council of Constantinople, which profoundly shaped later Byzantine theology.
